blocks.title: Sequence homology
blocks.text: Sequence homology is the similarity between DNA, RNA or protein sequences due to shared ancestry. Homologous sequences have evolved from a common ancestral sequence.

Homologous sequences fall into two main types. Orthologs are sequences in different species that originated from a common ancestral gene during speciation; orthologs often retain the same function across species. Paralogs are sequences within the same species that originated by gene duplication; paralogs can evolve new functions even though they arose from the same ancestral gene.

Sequence homology gives insight into the evolutionary relationships between organisms: by comparing homologous sequences, scientists can infer the evolutionary history and divergence of species. It also gives a clue to the function of an unknown gene or protein: if an unknown gene or protein is homologous to one with a known function, it is likely to have a similar function. And identifying homologous genes involved in diseases across different species helps in understanding disease mechanisms and developing treatments, since homologous genes in model organisms can be studied to gain insight into human diseases.

blocks.title: Structural homology
blocks.text: Structural homology is the similarity in the three-dimensional structures of proteins or other macromolecules due to shared ancestry. Proteins with similar structures often perform similar functions, even if their sequences are not highly similar.

The three-dimensional structure of a protein gives critical information about its function, so understanding structural homology helps in predicting the function of newly discovered proteins. It is crucial in drug design, because drugs are often designed to interact with specific protein structures, and understanding the structural relationships between proteins helps in designing more effective drugs. Studying the structural homology of proteins also helps in understanding the evolutionary processes that shape protein functions and interactions.

blocks.alt: Left: an ancestral gene splits by speciation into gene A in species 1 and gene A in species 2, linked by a dashed line labelled orthologs; gene A in species 1 then duplicates into gene A and gene A prime, labelled paralogs. Right: two proteins of different colour with different letter sequences beneath but the same ribbon fold inside, labelled structural homology.
blocks.caption: Orthologs and paralogs, and structural homology (original diagram after Figures 7.6 and 7.7).
blocks.long_description: Orthologs are versions of the same ancestral gene in different species, separated by speciation and usually keeping the same function. Paralogs are copies of a gene within one species made by gene duplication, which may evolve new functions. Structural homology is a shared three-dimensional fold inherited from a common ancestor; two proteins with quite different sequences can share the fold and therefore the function. The sequences and shapes drawn are schematic.

blocks.prompt: Two proteins share only a little of their amino acid sequence but fold into the same shape and both bind the same drug. Which kind of homology explains this, and what does it suggest about their function and ancestry?
blocks.explanation: Structural homology: their three-dimensional folds are alike because they descend from a common ancestral protein, even though their sequences have diverged. Similar structure suggests similar function, which is why the same drug fits both and why structural relationships guide drug design.

items: Sequence homology is similarity of DNA, RNA or protein sequences from shared ancestry: orthologs (different species, speciation, same function) and paralogs (same species, gene duplication, may gain new functions).
It reveals evolutionary relationships, predicts the function of unknown genes, and links disease genes in model organisms to human disease.

Structural homology is similarity of 3D structure from shared ancestry; similar structure usually means similar function, even with different sequences. It predicts function, guides drug design and traces the evolution of proteins.
